heading: Translucent vs transparent
question: Glass is transparent and frosted glass is translucent. Explain the difference using how light passes through.
answer: A transparent material lets nearly all the light pass straight through, so we can see clearly through it (like clear glass). A translucent material lets some light through but scatters it, so we can see light but not a clear image — shapes appear blurred (like frosted glass).
keywords: transparent: all light through, see clearly; translucent: some light scattered, blurred image

heading: Why shadow forms
question: Explain why a shadow forms behind an opaque object placed in front of a torch.
answer: Light from the torch travels in straight lines. The opaque object blocks the light (no light passes through). Behind the object, on the side away from the torch, no light reaches the surface — this area is dark and forms a shadow. The shape of the shadow matches the outline of the object because light travels in straight lines.
keywords: light in straight lines, opaque blocks light, no light behind, dark area forms shadow

heading: Magnet — opposites attract
question: When the north pole of one magnet is brought close to the south pole of another magnet, what happens? Explain.
answer: The two magnets attract each other. The rule is: unlike poles attract, like poles repel. So a north pole and a south pole (which are unlike) pull toward each other and the magnets stick together.
keywords: unlike poles attract, like poles repel, north to south, magnets stick

heading: Magnet picks up paper clips
question: A teacher passes a magnet over a tray with paper clips, pins and pencils. The magnet picks up only some objects. Explain.
answer: Magnets only attract magnetic materials, mainly iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Paper clips and pins are made of steel, so they are attracted. Pencils are made of wood and graphite, which are non-magnetic, so they are not attracted. Magnets do not attract everything — only magnetic materials.
keywords: magnets attract magnetic materials, iron steel nickel cobalt, paper clips attracted, pencils non-magnetic

heading: Strongest part of magnet
question: Where is a magnet strongest? How can you show this with iron filings?
answer: A magnet is strongest at its two poles (the ends). If iron filings are sprinkled near a bar magnet, the most filings stick at the ends (the poles), and very few cling near the middle. This shows that the magnetic force is strongest at the poles.
keywords: strongest at poles, ends of magnet, iron filings cluster at ends, fewer in middle

heading: Making a magnet — stroking
question: How can you make an iron nail into a magnet using another magnet?
answer: Stroke the nail many times in the same direction, with one pole of the magnet, from one end of the nail to the other. After many strokes, the nail becomes a magnet. This is called the stroking method.
keywords: stroke same direction, one pole, many times, nail becomes magnet, stroking method

heading: Demagnetising a magnet
question: State two ways a magnet can lose its magnetism.
answer: A magnet can lose its magnetism if it is (1) dropped or hammered hard, or (2) heated strongly. Both actions disturb the alignment of the magnetic particles inside the magnet so it no longer behaves as a magnet.
keywords: drop or hammer, heat strongly, disturbs alignment, loses magnetism

heading: States of matter — solids
question: Describe two properties of a solid that make it different from a liquid.
answer: A solid has its own fixed shape — it keeps the same shape no matter what container it is in. A solid also has a fixed volume. A liquid, by contrast, has no fixed shape (it takes the shape of the container) although it has a fixed volume. So solids are firmer and hold their shape, while liquids flow.
keywords: solid: fixed shape and volume; liquid: takes container shape, fixed volume

heading: Why gas fills container
question: When a balloon is blown up, the gas spreads out to fill the whole balloon. Explain why.
answer: A gas has no fixed shape and no fixed volume — its particles are far apart and move freely in all directions. So when air is blown into the balloon, the gas particles spread out and fill the entire balloon space evenly. This is why a gas always takes the shape and volume of its container.
keywords: gas: no fixed shape or volume, particles move freely, fills whole container

heading: Measure liquid volume
question: Describe how you would measure the volume of some water.
answer: Pour the water carefully into a measuring cylinder placed on a flat surface. Look at the water level with your eye at the same level as the surface of the water. Read the scale at the bottom of the curved water surface (the meniscus). The reading gives the volume in cm³ or millilitres (ml).
keywords: use measuring cylinder, flat surface, eye level, read at meniscus, in ml or cm3

heading: Measure irregular solid volume
question: How would you find the volume of a small irregular stone?
answer: Half-fill a measuring cylinder with water and read the volume (V1). Carefully lower the stone into the water until it is completely submerged. Read the new water level (V2). The volume of the stone is V2 − V1 — the amount of water it displaced. This is the displacement method.
keywords: measuring cylinder with water, V1; lower stone, V2; volume = V2 minus V1; displacement

heading: Plant parts — function of root
question: State two functions of the roots of a plant.
answer: First, the roots anchor the plant in the ground so it stays upright and is not blown away. Second, the roots absorb water and dissolved mineral salts from the soil, which the plant needs to grow.
keywords: anchor in ground, absorb water and mineral salts

heading: Function of stem
question: Explain two roles played by the stem of a flowering plant.
answer: The stem holds the plant upright so the leaves and flowers are in sunlight. The stem also contains tube-like vessels that transport water and minerals up from the roots to the leaves, and transport food made in the leaves down to the rest of the plant.
keywords: holds plant upright, leaves get sunlight, transports water and food

heading: Why do plants need leaves
question: Why are leaves important for a plant?
answer: Leaves are where the plant makes its own food, by photosynthesis. They are usually flat and broad to catch a lot of sunlight. They contain chlorophyll (the green substance) which captures sunlight, and tiny pores called stomata which let gases pass in and out.
keywords: make food, photosynthesis, broad to catch sunlight, chlorophyll, stomata for gas exchange

heading: Plant needs water — wilting
question: If a plant is not watered for several days, its leaves become limp and droop. Explain why.
answer: Without water from the soil, the plant cannot replace the water lost from its leaves (by transpiration). The plant's cells lose water, so they become limp and the stem and leaves can no longer hold themselves up. This is called wilting. If watered in time, the plant takes up water again and the leaves stand up firm.
keywords: no water from soil, cells lose water, become limp, wilting, leaves and stem droop

heading: Living vs non-living characteristics
question: Name three characteristics that living things have but non-living things do not have.
answer: Living things: (1) grow and develop over time, (2) reproduce — make more of themselves, (3) need food/energy to live, (4) respond to changes around them, (5) breathe (gas exchange), (6) get rid of waste. Non-living things do not do any of these on their own.
keywords: grow, reproduce, need food, respond, breathe, get rid of waste

heading: Why is a car not living
question: A car moves and uses fuel. Why is a car still considered non-living?
answer: Even though a car moves and uses fuel, it does not have all the characteristics of living things. A car cannot grow by itself, cannot make more cars (reproduce), cannot breathe, and cannot respond by itself to its surroundings. So a car is non-living, even though it moves.
keywords: car moves but cannot grow, cannot reproduce, cannot breathe on its own, non-living

heading: Plants are living — examples
question: Give three reasons why a plant is a living thing.
answer: A plant is living because it (1) grows bigger over time, (2) reproduces by making seeds, (3) needs food (it makes its own using sunlight), (4) responds — for example, its stem turns toward light. It also takes in gases for photosynthesis and respiration.
keywords: grows, reproduces by seeds, makes food, responds to light, takes in gases

heading: Vertebrate vs invertebrate
question: What is the main difference between a vertebrate and an invertebrate? Give one example of each.
answer: A vertebrate is an animal with a backbone. An invertebrate is an animal without a backbone. Examples: vertebrate — fish, bird, dog, frog, snake. Invertebrate — insect (butterfly, ant), spider, worm, snail.
keywords: vertebrate has backbone, invertebrate has no backbone, examples

heading: Flowering vs non-flowering plant
question: How is a flowering plant different from a non-flowering plant?
answer: A flowering plant produces flowers, and from the flowers it makes seeds for reproduction. A non-flowering plant does not produce flowers; it reproduces by spores (like ferns and mosses) or by cones (like pine trees). Both are still living plants.
keywords: flowering has flowers and seeds, non-flowering: spores or cones, ferns mosses pines

heading: Mammals — common features
question: Name two features that all mammals share.
answer: All mammals have fur or hair on their bodies, and all mammals feed their young with milk from the mother's body. Most mammals also give birth to live young (not eggs). Examples: dog, cat, dolphin, human.
keywords: fur or hair, feed young with milk, give birth to live young, examples

heading: Why classify living things
question: Why do scientists put living things into groups?
answer: Grouping (classifying) helps scientists study living things more easily — once we know which group an animal or plant belongs to, we know many things about it (what it eats, how it moves, how it reproduces) without studying it from scratch. It also helps us identify new living things and see relationships between them.
keywords: easier to study, know features from group, identify new ones, see relationships

heading: Habitat — definition
question: What is a habitat? Give one example.
answer: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives. The habitat gives the living thing what it needs — food, water, air and shelter. For example, the habitat of a fish is the river or sea; the habitat of a bee is a garden or forest near flowers.
keywords: place where it lives, gives food water shelter, fish in sea, bee in garden

heading: Fungi vs plants
question: How are fungi different from plants, even though both are not animals?
answer: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, using sunlight. Fungi cannot make their own food — they grow on dead or decaying matter and absorb nutrients from it. Fungi also do not have leaves, stems, roots or flowers. Examples of fungi: mushrooms, mould, yeast.
keywords: plants make food by photosynthesis, fungi cannot, fungi grow on dead matter, no leaves or roots

heading: Why bacteria important
question: Are bacteria living things? Why are they important?
answer: Yes, bacteria are living — they grow, reproduce and need food. Most bacteria are tiny (microscopic) and many are helpful: they break down dead plants and animals (decomposition), help our digestion in our gut, and are used to make foods like yoghurt. A few types cause disease.
keywords: bacteria living, decomposers, help digestion, make yoghurt, some cause disease

heading: Photosynthesis happens where
question: In which part of the plant does photosynthesis mainly take place? Why?
answer: Photosynthesis mainly takes place in the leaves. Leaves are flat and broad, so they have a large surface to absorb sunlight. They are also packed with chlorophyll, the green substance that traps sunlight. Stomata on the leaf allow carbon dioxide to enter and oxygen to leave.
keywords: in the leaves, broad and flat, chlorophyll traps sunlight, stomata for gases

heading: Plant also respires
question: Many students think plants only photosynthesise. Explain why this is wrong.
answer: Plants also respire — just like animals. Respiration happens day and night in plant cells, using oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide, to release energy from food. Photosynthesis, however, only happens when there is light. So during the day a plant does both, but at night the plant only respires.
keywords: plants respire day and night, photosynthesis only in light, day: both, night: only respire

heading: Why night plants bad for sleeping
question: Some people say that having many plants in a closed bedroom at night is not very healthy. Explain using science.
answer: At night there is no light, so plants do not photosynthesise — they only respire. Respiration uses up oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide. In a closed bedroom, many plants can lower the oxygen level and raise the carbon dioxide level slightly. In a normal home with open ventilation this is not dangerous.
keywords: no light at night, no photosynthesis, only respire, use oxygen, give out CO₂

heading: Cells — building block of life
question: Why are cells described as 'the building blocks of life'?
answer: All living things — plants, animals, fungi, bacteria — are made of cells. A cell is the smallest part of a living thing that can carry out the functions of life. Many tiny cells join together to form tissues, then organs, then a whole body. So just like blocks build a wall, cells build every living thing.
keywords: smallest unit of life, all living things made of cells, build tissues organs body

heading: Plant cell vs animal cell
question: State two ways a plant cell is different from an animal cell.
answer: A plant cell has a cell wall (in addition to the cell membrane), which gives it shape and rigidity; an animal cell does not. A plant cell also has chloroplasts (which contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis); an animal cell does not. A plant cell often has a large central vacuole.
keywords: plant: cell wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole; animal: only membrane, no chloroplasts

heading: Why is variation important
question: Most living things show variation — small differences within the same species. Why is variation important for survival?
answer: Variation means some members of the species have features slightly different from others. If the environment changes (e.g. a disease, climate change), some individuals may have features that let them survive better, while others die. The survivors pass their useful features to their offspring. Without variation, a whole species could be wiped out by one change.
keywords: differences within species, some better suited, survive change, pass features to offspring, prevents extinction

heading: Inherited vs acquired
question: What is the difference between an inherited characteristic and an acquired characteristic? Give one example of each.
answer: Inherited characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through reproduction — for example, eye colour, blood type, fingerprint pattern. Acquired characteristics are picked up during a person's lifetime due to environment or experience — for example, a scar from an injury, the ability to ride a bike. Acquired characteristics are not passed to offspring.
keywords: inherited: from parents, eye colour, blood type; acquired: during life, scar, bike skill

heading: Carnivore teeth adaptation
question: Lions have long, sharp canine teeth and large molars. Explain how these are adaptations for the way they live.
answer: Lions are carnivores — they hunt and eat meat. Long, sharp canine teeth pierce and grip the prey when caught, holding it firmly. Large strong molars at the back of the mouth crush and slice meat and bone. These tooth adaptations let lions catch and eat their prey, which is essential for their survival.
keywords: carnivore, long canines pierce and grip prey, large molars crush meat, helps hunt and eat

heading: Camouflage — definition + example
question: What is camouflage? Give one example and explain how it helps the animal survive.
answer: Camouflage is when an animal's colour or pattern blends with its surroundings, making it hard to see. Example: a green grasshopper sitting on grass is hard for a bird (predator) to spot, so it is less likely to be eaten. For a predator, camouflage helps it sneak up on prey without being seen. So camouflage helps with both hunting and escaping.
keywords: blends with surroundings, hard to see, hides from predator or sneaks up on prey, helps survive

heading: Why dew on grass in morning
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: Early in the morning, dew is often found on grass and leaves. Explain how the dew formed.
answer: During the night, the grass and leaves cool down quickly. Water vapour in the air around the cold grass loses heat and condenses into tiny water droplets on the leaves. These droplets are dew. So dew forms by condensation when warm moist air meets a cold surface.
keywords: grass cools at night, water vapour cools, condenses on cold leaves, droplets are dew

heading: Why washing dries faster on sunny day
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: Wet clothes hung outdoors dry faster on a hot, windy day than on a cool, still day. Explain why.
answer: Drying is evaporation — water in the clothes turns into water vapour. Evaporation is faster when (a) the surroundings are hotter, because more heat energy reaches the water and turns it into vapour faster, and (b) when there is wind, because moving air carries the water vapour away quickly, leaving room for more to evaporate.
keywords: evaporation faster when hotter, more heat energy; wind carries vapour away, faster drying

heading: Boiling vs evaporation
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: How is boiling different from evaporation?
answer: Both are changes from liquid to gas. Boiling happens only at a fixed temperature (the boiling point of the liquid), and bubbles of gas form inside the liquid. Evaporation happens at any temperature, only at the surface of the liquid (no bubbles), and is slower than boiling.
keywords: boiling: fixed temperature, bubbles inside, fast; evaporation: any temperature, surface only, slower

heading: Why water cycle never ends
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: Explain why the water on Earth never runs out, even though water is constantly being used.
answer: The water cycle keeps recycling water. Water evaporates from seas, rivers and lakes (and from leaves and our bodies) into the air as water vapour. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds. Eventually it falls back to Earth as rain, snow or hail (precipitation). The same water is used over and over.
keywords: water cycle, evaporation, condensation, precipitation, water recycled and never runs out

heading: Weight vs mass
question: A student says 'my mass on the Moon is the same as on Earth, but my weight is different'. Is this correct? Explain.
answer: Yes, this is correct. Mass is the amount of matter in the body — it does not change with location, so it is the same on Earth and on the Moon. Weight is the force of gravity on the body. The Moon's gravity is much weaker than Earth's, so the same person has less weight on the Moon, even though the mass is the same.
keywords: mass = amount of matter, same everywhere; weight = force of gravity, less on Moon

heading: Why parachute slows fall
question: A skydiver opens his parachute. Explain why his fall slows down after the parachute opens.
answer: When the parachute opens, the parachute has a very large surface area facing the air. This creates a large air resistance force pushing upward against the skydiver's motion. The upward air resistance becomes nearly equal to the downward gravitational force on the skydiver. With balanced forces, the skydiver no longer speeds up and falls gently.
keywords: parachute large surface, lots of air resistance upward, balances gravity, falls slowly

heading: Why rocket needs huge fuel
question: Rockets need huge amounts of fuel to leave Earth. Why?
answer: Earth's gravity pulls everything down very strongly. For a rocket to escape into space, its engines must push it upward with a force much greater than Earth's gravitational pull, for a long time. Producing such a huge force takes a huge amount of fuel — most of the rocket's weight at launch is actually fuel.
keywords: Earth's gravity strong, need huge upward force to overcome, need huge amount of fuel

heading: Why dam stores energy
question: Water held in a dam high up a mountain is used to make electricity. Describe the energy conversions that take place.
answer: The water held high up has gravitational potential energy (GPE) because of its height. When released, this GPE is converted into kinetic energy (KE) as the water rushes downward. The fast-moving water turns turbines, converting the kinetic energy into mechanical (rotating) energy. The turbines drive a generator, which converts the mechanical energy into electrical energy.
keywords: GPE high water, converts to KE as falls, turns turbines (mechanical), generator makes electrical energy

heading: Solar to electricity
question: Explain how solar panels on a roof produce electricity for the house, in energy terms.
answer: Solar panels receive light energy from the Sun. Inside the panels, the light energy is converted directly into electrical energy, which is then used to power the house. So the energy conversion is light energy → electrical energy.
keywords: solar panel, light from Sun, light energy to electrical energy, powers house

heading: Stretched spring energy
question: A toy has a spring that is wound up tight. When released, the toy moves. Describe the energy changes.
answer: When the spring is wound up, it stores elastic potential energy. When released, this elastic potential energy is converted into kinetic energy that makes the toy move. Some energy is also lost to friction (as heat) and air resistance (sometimes as sound), so the toy eventually slows down and stops.
keywords: wound spring: elastic PE; release: kinetic, makes toy move; some lost to friction as heat

heading: Why metal expands when heated
question: Why does a metal bar become slightly longer when it is heated?
answer: When the metal is heated, the particles inside gain heat energy and vibrate faster. They take up more space as they vibrate more, so the metal expands and becomes slightly longer. When it cools, the particles slow down and the metal contracts back.
keywords: particles gain energy, vibrate faster, take more space, metal expands

heading: Why bridges have gaps
question: Bridges and railway tracks often have small gaps between sections. Explain why.
answer: Metal expands when heated. On a hot day, the metal sections of the bridge or track expand and become slightly longer. The gaps give space for this expansion, so the sections do not push hard against each other and buckle (bend). On cold days, the metal contracts and the gaps become larger.
keywords: metal expands when hot, gaps allow expansion, prevent buckling, contracts when cold

heading: Thermometer works how
question: Explain how a liquid-in-glass thermometer measures temperature.
answer: The thermometer is a thin glass tube containing a liquid (often alcohol or mercury). When the surroundings are hotter, the liquid gains heat and expands, rising up the tube. When cooler, it contracts and falls. The level of the liquid against a marked scale tells us the temperature.
keywords: liquid expands when hot, rises up tube, scale shows temperature, contracts when cold

heading: Why wood is poor conductor
question: Wooden spoons are often used to stir hot soup. Why?
answer: Wood is a poor conductor of heat. When you stir hot soup with a wooden spoon, heat takes a long time to pass up the handle to your hand. So the handle stays cool enough to hold. A metal spoon, being a good conductor, would quickly become hot and could burn the hand.
keywords: wood poor conductor, heat passes slowly, handle stays cool, safe to hold

heading: Why thermos keeps drink warm
question: A thermos flask can keep a drink hot for hours. Explain how.
answer: A thermos flask has a double-walled container with a vacuum (no air) between the walls. Since heat needs particles to travel through, the vacuum stops heat passing in or out. The outside cap is also a poor conductor. So heat from the hot drink cannot easily escape, and the drink stays hot for a long time.
keywords: double wall, vacuum no particles, heat cannot pass, poor conductor cap, drink stays hot

heading: Sunglasses block light
question: How do dark sunglasses help on a sunny day?
answer: The dark lenses of sunglasses absorb a large amount of the light that comes into them. So less light enters the eyes. This makes bright sunlight more comfortable to look at and reduces glare. Some sunglasses also block ultraviolet light, which can harm the eyes.
keywords: dark lenses absorb light, less light into eye, reduces glare, protects from UV

heading: Why shadow gets bigger
question: A boy stands between a lamp and a wall. When he steps closer to the lamp, his shadow on the wall becomes bigger. Explain.
answer: Light from the lamp spreads out in straight lines as it travels. When the boy moves closer to the lamp, he blocks a larger cone of light, so the dark area (shadow) on the wall is bigger. Moving away from the lamp blocks a smaller cone, so the shadow is smaller.
keywords: light spreads in straight lines, closer to lamp blocks bigger cone, bigger shadow

heading: Sun is light source
question: Why is the Sun called a source of light, but the Moon is not?
answer: A light source is something that produces its own light. The Sun is very hot and produces its own light (from nuclear reactions). The Moon does not produce its own light — it only reflects sunlight, which is why we can see it. So the Sun is a light source, but the Moon is not.
keywords: source: produces its own light; Sun produces light, Moon reflects sunlight, not a source

heading: Plants need sunlight — investigation
question: A student wants to find out if plants need sunlight to grow. Describe an experiment she could do.
answer: Take two similar plants in similar pots. Put one in a bright sunny spot, and put the other in a dark cupboard. Water both equally. Observe over a few days. The plant in sunlight will stay green and healthy; the one in the dark will turn yellow and weak. This shows plants need sunlight to grow.
keywords: two similar plants, one in sun one in dark, water equally, observe over days

heading: Animal characteristics — definition
question: Why is a butterfly a living thing? Give two reasons.
answer: A butterfly is living because it (1) needs food (nectar) to live, (2) grows from a caterpillar into an adult, (3) reproduces by laying eggs, (4) moves and responds to its surroundings, (5) breathes air. Any two of these are enough to show it is living.
keywords: needs food, grows, reproduces, moves and responds, breathes

heading: Compare plant and animal
question: State two ways plants and animals are similar, and two ways they are different.
answer: Similarities: both are living things, both need water and air, both grow and reproduce, both respond to surroundings. Differences: plants make their own food by photosynthesis; animals must eat other living things. Plants stay rooted in one place; animals can move around.
keywords: similar: both living, need water and air, grow, reproduce; different: plants make food, stay rooted; animals eat, move

heading: Identify a non-living thing
question: A student lists: a rock, a tree, a cloud, a fish. Which is non-living and how can you tell?
answer: The rock and the cloud are non-living. We can tell because a rock and a cloud do not grow on their own, do not eat or breathe, do not reproduce, and do not respond to their surroundings. The tree and the fish are living because they show all of these characteristics.
keywords: rock and cloud non-living, do not grow eat breathe reproduce, tree and fish are living

heading: Fish — habitat features
question: Why is a fish well-suited to life in water?
answer: A fish has a streamlined (slim) body so it can move through water easily. It has fins to help it swim and steer. It has gills to take in oxygen from the water. Its body is covered in slimy scales that reduce friction with the water and protect it. All these features make it well-suited to a water habitat.
keywords: streamlined body, fins to swim, gills for oxygen in water, slimy scales reduce friction

heading: Why birds have wings
question: Birds have wings and hollow bones. How do these features help them?
answer: Wings let birds fly — this helps them travel far to find food, escape predators on the ground, and reach high places to nest. Hollow bones make birds light, which means less energy is needed to fly. So wings + light bones together let birds live in the sky.
keywords: wings let birds fly, hollow bones make light, less energy to fly, escape predators, find food

heading: Why fur on polar bear
question: A polar bear has very thick fur and a layer of fat under its skin. Explain how these help it survive in the Arctic.
answer: Thick fur and a layer of fat are both poor conductors of heat. Together they stop heat from leaving the bear's body. This keeps the bear warm in the very cold Arctic, where temperatures are well below freezing. Without these features the bear would lose body heat too quickly and freeze.
keywords: thick fur, fat layer, poor conductors of heat, keep bear warm in Arctic

heading: Habitat — desert plants
question: How is a cactus suited to life in the desert?
answer: A cactus has thick fleshy stems that store water for long dry periods. Its leaves are tiny spines, which reduces water loss and protects the plant from animals. Its roots spread wide and shallow to collect any rainwater quickly. These adaptations help the cactus survive where there is very little water.
keywords: fleshy stem stores water, spine-leaves reduce water loss, wide roots collect rain

heading: Ring-barking experiment
question: A scientist cuts a ring of bark off a tree trunk, removing the outer ring of food-carrying tubes. Predict what will happen to the leaves and roots over the next few weeks. Explain.
answer: The leaves above the cut will still get water and minerals from the roots through the water-carrying tubes (which are not removed), so they keep doing photosynthesis. The roots, however, no longer receive food from the leaves (food-tubes are cut). Without food, the roots cannot grow or function and will slowly die. The whole tree eventually dies.
keywords: food-tubes removed, leaves still get water, roots no longer get food, roots starve and die

heading: Transpiration definition
question: What is transpiration, and where in the plant does it mainly happen?
answer: Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant in the form of water vapour. It mainly happens through tiny pores called stomata on the underside of leaves. The water inside the leaves evaporates into the air around the plant, and this loss pulls more water up from the roots.
keywords: loss of water vapour, mainly through stomata on leaves, water evaporates

heading: Faster transpiration when
question: Under what conditions does a plant lose water faster by transpiration?
answer: A plant transpires faster when (1) it is hot — heat speeds up evaporation; (2) it is windy — wind carries water vapour away quickly; (3) the air is dry (low humidity) — more room for water vapour; (4) it has many leaves — more stomata.
keywords: faster when hot, windy, dry air, many leaves

heading: Why guard cells
question: Beside each stoma in a leaf are two special cells called guard cells. What is their job?
answer: Guard cells open and close the stoma. When the plant has plenty of water and needs to do photosynthesis, the guard cells swell and open the stoma, letting carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. When the plant is short of water, the guard cells go limp and close the stoma to reduce water loss.
keywords: guard cells open/close stoma, open for photosynthesis, close to save water

heading: Mosses — non-flowering plant
question: How does a moss reproduce, even though it does not have flowers?
answer: Mosses reproduce by spores, not seeds. They produce tiny spore-cases that release thousands of light spores into the air. When spores land in a damp, suitable place, they grow into new moss plants. So even without flowers and seeds, mosses can multiply and spread.
keywords: spores not seeds, light spores carried by air, land in damp place, grow into new moss

heading: Ferns characteristics
question: What kind of plant is a fern? How does it reproduce?
answer: A fern is a non-flowering plant. It has roots, stems and leaves (called fronds), but it does not produce flowers or seeds. Ferns reproduce by spores produced on the underside of their fronds. When spores fall to a damp place, they grow into new ferns.
keywords: non-flowering, no seeds, reproduces by spores under fronds, damp place

heading: Why protect endangered species
question: Why is it important for humans to protect endangered animals from extinction?
answer: Every species plays a role in its habitat (e.g. in food chains). If one species goes extinct, the whole food chain is affected — other animals lose food or lose their predators. Some species are also sources of food or medicine for humans. Once a species is extinct, it cannot be brought back. So protecting endangered species protects the balance of nature and benefits humans too.
keywords: every species has role, extinction affects food chain, lose food or medicine, cannot be reversed

heading: Recycle reduce reuse
question: Explain the meaning of 'reduce', 'reuse' and 'recycle' and give one example of each.
answer: Reduce means use less of something — e.g. switch off lights you don't need to use less electricity. Reuse means use the same item again — e.g. use the same water bottle every day instead of buying new bottles. Recycle means treat used items so they can be made into new things — e.g. paper recycled into new paper. All three reduce waste and save resources.
keywords: reduce: use less, switch off lights; reuse: same item again, water bottle; recycle: make into new, paper

heading: Why oil spill is harmful
question: An oil tanker leaks oil into the sea. Explain two ways this is harmful to sea creatures.

heading: Why animals need to drink
question: Why do humans and other animals need to drink water?
answer: Water is needed for our blood to flow properly, for digesting food, for cooling the body by sweating, and for getting rid of waste in urine. Without enough water, the body becomes weak (dehydrated). We need to keep drinking water every day to replace what we lose.
keywords: blood flow, digestion, sweating cools, removes waste, replace water lost

heading: Why woolly clothes warm
question: Why does wearing a thick woollen jacket keep you warm in cold weather?
answer: Wool fibres trap a lot of air. Air is a very poor conductor of heat. So the trapped air stops heat from your body escaping into the cold air outside. The thicker the wool, the more trapped air, and the warmer you stay.
keywords: wool traps air, air poor conductor, stops heat leaving body, stays warm

heading: Aluminium foil and food
question: Why is hot food sometimes wrapped in aluminium foil to keep it warm?
answer: Aluminium foil is shiny and reflects radiated heat back toward the food. The foil also acts as a barrier so air cannot carry heat away easily. Together, these slow down heat loss from the food, so the food stays warmer for longer.
keywords: shiny reflects heat back, blocks air movement, slows heat loss, food stays warm

heading: Why aircon room cool
question: An air-conditioner makes a room cool. Where does the heat go?
answer: The air conditioner takes heat from the room air and moves it outside the building. Inside the air-con unit, a special liquid absorbs heat from the room and then releases it outside. So the room cools down because heat is removed and dumped outside.
keywords: air-con takes heat from room, special liquid absorbs heat, releases heat outside

heading: Reflection mirror
question: How does a flat mirror let you see your face?
answer: Light from the lamps in the room hits your face and reflects off it. That reflected light then travels to the mirror, hits the smooth mirror surface, and reflects again into your eye. Because the mirror surface is very flat and smooth, the reflection looks like a clear image of your face.
keywords: light bounces off face, hits smooth mirror, reflects to eye, clear image

heading: Why white paper bright
question: Why does white paper look much brighter under a lamp than black paper?
answer: White paper reflects nearly all the light that falls on it — most of it bounces off into our eyes. Black paper absorbs nearly all the light and reflects very little, so very little reaches our eyes. That is why white looks bright and black looks dark.
keywords: white reflects most light, black absorbs light, more light to eye from white

heading: Why nail rust
question: Iron nails left outside become rusty. Explain what causes rust.
answer: Rust forms when iron is in contact with both water and oxygen (from the air). The water and oxygen react slowly with the iron to form a new orange-brown substance called rust. Rust weakens the iron. To prevent rust, we can paint, oil or coat the iron with another metal.
keywords: iron plus water plus oxygen, slow reaction, forms rust, prevent with paint or oil

heading: Why container shape matters
question: When designing a cup, why does it matter that water has no fixed shape?
answer: Because water has no fixed shape, it will take whatever shape the container is. So a cup must be designed to hold the water — with walls and a bottom — otherwise water would just spread out. The designer chooses the shape, but the water simply takes that shape.
keywords: water takes container shape, cup must hold water in, design controls shape

heading: Three states of water demo
question: Describe a simple way to show all three states of water in one experiment.
answer: Put a few ice cubes (solid) in a beaker on a tripod. Heat the beaker. The ice melts to liquid water. Continue heating until the water boils — water vapour (gas) rises from the surface. Hold a cold lid above the steam: the vapour cools and condenses back to liquid water on the lid. Solid → liquid → gas → liquid is shown.
keywords: ice solid, melts to liquid, boils to gas (vapour), condenses back to liquid on lid

heading: Producers definition
question: What is a producer in a food chain? Give an example.
answer: A producer is a living thing that makes its own food, using energy from the Sun. Green plants are producers — they use photosynthesis to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Producers are always at the start of a food chain because they bring energy from the Sun into the food chain.
keywords: makes own food, uses sunlight, green plants, start of food chain

heading: Primary consumer
question: What is a primary consumer? Give an example using a food chain.
answer: A primary consumer is an animal that eats producers (plants). It is the second link in a food chain. For example, in 'grass → grasshopper → frog → snake', the grasshopper is the primary consumer because it eats the grass (producer).
keywords: eats producers, second in chain, grasshopper eats grass

heading: Why food web safer
question: Why is it 'safer' for animals to be part of a food web than a single food chain?
answer: In a food web, an animal can have several different food sources, and there are many overlapping food chains. If one food source disappears, the animal can switch to another. In a single chain, if one link is lost, the animals above it have nothing to eat. So a food web makes a habitat more stable.
keywords: many food sources, can switch if one disappears, habitat more stable, single chain breaks

heading: Food web — arrow meaning
question: In a food chain, an arrow points from the grass to the rabbit. What does this arrow mean?
answer: The arrow shows the direction in which energy flows. The arrow goes from the food (grass) to the eater (rabbit), because energy from the grass passes into the rabbit when the rabbit eats the grass. So 'A → B' means energy goes from A into B; in other words, B eats A.
keywords: arrow shows energy flow, points from food to eater, B eats A

heading: Solar lamp energy
question: A solar garden lamp charges in the day and lights up at night. Describe the energy conversions.
answer: During the day: light energy from the Sun is absorbed by the solar panel and converted into electrical energy. The electrical energy is stored in a battery as chemical energy. At night: chemical energy in the battery converts back to electrical energy, which is then converted by the bulb into light energy (and a little heat).
keywords: Sun: light to electrical to chemical (battery); night: chemical to electrical to light

heading: Wind turbine
question: Explain how a wind turbine produces electricity. List the main energy conversions.
answer: Wind has kinetic energy (moving air). The wind pushes the turbine blades, which turn. So the wind's kinetic energy becomes the kinetic energy of the spinning blades. The blades turn a generator that converts the rotation into electrical energy. So the chain is: kinetic (wind) → kinetic (blades) → electrical.
keywords: kinetic wind, turns blades, kinetic spinning, generator makes electrical energy

heading: Speaker energy
question: When a song plays from your phone speaker, what energy conversion takes place inside the speaker?
answer: The phone sends an electrical signal to the speaker. The speaker converts the electrical energy into sound energy by vibrating a thin membrane (cone). The vibration shakes the air, producing sound waves that we hear.
keywords: electrical signal into speaker, converted to sound, vibrating cone shakes air

heading: Kettle energy
question: When water boils in an electric kettle, what are the main energy conversions?
answer: Electrical energy flows into the kettle from the wall socket. The heating element inside converts the electrical energy into heat energy. The heat is transferred to the water, raising its temperature until it boils. (A little sound is also produced as the water boils.)
keywords: electrical to heat in element, heat to water, water boils, also some sound

heading: Why pupa important
question: Why is the pupa stage important in a butterfly's life cycle, even though the butterfly does not eat or move much during it?
answer: Inside the pupa, the body of the caterpillar is broken down and rebuilt into a butterfly. New organs (like wings) are formed during this resting stage. Without the pupa stage, the caterpillar could not change into the adult butterfly. So the pupa is a stage of major change (metamorphosis).
keywords: body rebuilt inside pupa, new organs form (like wings), metamorphosis to adult

heading: Bird life cycle
question: Describe the simple stages in the life cycle of a bird, e.g. a chicken.
answer: The female lays a fertilised egg with a hard shell. Inside the egg, the chick develops, fed by the yolk. After about three weeks the chick hatches out. The young chick grows by eating food until it is fully grown. The adult bird mates and lays its own eggs, and the cycle repeats.
keywords: egg laid, chick develops inside, hatches, grows on food, adult mates and lays eggs

heading: Mammal life cycle
question: How is the life cycle of a mammal, like a dog, different from a bird's?
answer: A mammal's young develops inside the mother (not in an egg). The mother gives birth to a young that already looks like a small version of the adult. The young is fed with milk from the mother's body and is cared for by the parent. In a bird, the young develops in an egg outside the mother's body and feeds itself or is fed worms etc., not milk.
keywords: mammal: young in mother, milk; bird: develops in egg, no milk, often fed by parent

heading: Plastic in ocean
question: Why is plastic rubbish in the ocean a serious problem for sea animals?
answer: Many sea animals (turtles, dolphins, fish, seabirds) mistake plastic for food and swallow it. Plastic is not digested and fills up the stomach, so the animal feels full but starves to death. Animals can also become tangled in plastic bags and ropes and drown. Plastic also breaks into tiny pieces (microplastics) that enter food chains.
keywords: animals eat plastic, fills stomach, starve, get tangled, microplastics in food chain

heading: Why CO₂ a problem
question: Carbon dioxide is a natural part of the air, so why is too much of it a problem?
answer: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas. In small amounts it helps trap the right amount of heat to keep Earth warm. But humans are adding extra carbon dioxide by burning fossil fuels, so too much heat is trapped. Earth gets hotter, ice melts, sea levels rise, and weather becomes more extreme — this is global warming.
keywords: greenhouse gas, traps heat, too much CO₂ from burning fuel, Earth heats up, global warming

heading: Why save water Singapore
question: Even though Singapore has rain often, why is it important to save water?
answer: Singapore is a small country with no large rivers or lakes. Much of our water comes from rain caught in reservoirs and from imported water, NEWater and desalination. Producing and treating water uses energy and money. If everyone uses water wisely, the country can rely less on expensive sources and have enough water for the future.
keywords: small country, limited reservoirs, water treatment uses energy, save for future

heading: Air pollution sources
question: Give two main causes of air pollution in a city like Singapore, and one effect on people.
answer: Main causes: (1) vehicle exhaust from cars, buses and lorries; (2) smoke from factories and power stations burning fossil fuels; (3) sometimes haze from forest fires in nearby countries. One effect on people: breathing the polluted air can irritate the lungs and cause coughing, asthma attacks and other breathing problems.
keywords: vehicle exhaust, factory smoke, haze; causes coughing and asthma

heading: Coloured water in stem
question: A white flower is placed in water dyed with red ink. After several hours, the petals turn red. Explain.
answer: The red ink mixes with the water. The roots and cut stem take in the dyed water, which travels up the water-carrying tubes inside the stem to the petals. The ink stays in the petals and colours them red. This shows that water moves from roots to leaves and flowers through the stem.
keywords: dyed water taken up by stem, water-carrying tubes, reaches petals, colours them red

heading: How leaves help in transpiration
question: Explain how leaves are involved in transpiration.
answer: Water from the roots travels up the stem to the leaves. Inside the leaves, water turns into water vapour. The vapour escapes into the air through tiny pores (stomata) on the underside of the leaves. This loss of water vapour is transpiration. As water leaves, more water is pulled up from the roots.
keywords: water reaches leaves, becomes water vapour, escapes through stomata, pulls more water up

heading: Why fewer leaves wilt slower
question: Why do plants with fewer leaves often wilt less quickly in hot dry weather than plants with many leaves?
answer: Each leaf loses water by transpiration. A plant with many leaves loses water from many places at once, so it dries out fast. A plant with fewer leaves loses water from fewer places, so it dries out slower and wilts less quickly.
keywords: fewer leaves = less surface losing water, less transpiration, dries slower

heading: Plants that survive dry — feature
question: Name one feature of a plant that helps it survive in a dry place, and explain how it helps.
answer: Thick fleshy stems store water for later use. Some plants have small leaves or spines instead of broad leaves, which reduces the surface area for water loss. Some leaves have a waxy coating that stops water escaping. Each of these features reduces the amount of water the plant loses, so it can survive a long time without rain.
keywords: thick stem stores water, small leaves reduce loss, waxy coating, less water lost

heading: Cell membrane role
question: What is the role of the cell membrane in a cell?
answer: The cell membrane is a thin layer that surrounds the cell. It holds the cell contents together and controls what enters and leaves the cell — letting in useful things like food and oxygen, and letting out waste. It is like a careful gatekeeper for the cell.
keywords: thin layer around cell, controls what enters and leaves, holds cell together

heading: Nucleus role
question: The nucleus is found inside both plant and animal cells. What does it do?
answer: The nucleus controls everything that happens in the cell. It contains the genetic information (DNA), which tells the cell what to do and how to grow. Without a nucleus, the cell cannot control its activities and cannot divide to make new cells.
keywords: controls cell activities, contains genetic information (DNA), needed for cell division

heading: Cytoplasm role
question: What is cytoplasm and what happens there?
answer: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like fluid that fills most of the cell, between the cell membrane and the nucleus. Many of the cell's life activities (chemical reactions) happen in the cytoplasm — for example, the cell uses cytoplasm as the workspace to break down food and release energy.
keywords: jelly-like fluid inside cell, where most reactions happen, breaks down food

heading: Chloroplast role
question: What is the function of chloroplasts in plant cells?
answer: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green substance that captures sunlight. Photosynthesis happens inside the chloroplasts: light energy is used to combine carbon dioxide and water into sugar (food) and oxygen. Animal cells do not have chloroplasts because animals do not make their own food.
keywords: contain chlorophyll, photosynthesis happens inside, make sugar and oxygen

heading: Why animals have different food
question: Some animals eat only plants, some eat only meat, and some eat both. Give one example of each and what they are called.
answer: Animals that eat only plants are called herbivores — e.g. cow, rabbit, deer. Animals that eat only meat are called carnivores — e.g. lion, tiger, eagle. Animals that eat both plants and meat are called omnivores — e.g. humans, pigs, chickens.
keywords: herbivore eats plants, carnivore eats meat, omnivore eats both, examples

heading: How animals move differently
question: Different animals move in different ways. Give two examples of how animals move and link them to where they live.
answer: Fish swim, using fins and a tail — they live in water. Birds fly, using wings — they live in the air or in trees. Snakes slither using their muscles — they live on the ground. Each way of moving suits the animal's habitat.
keywords: fish swim with fins, bird fly with wings, snake slithers, way suits habitat

heading: Why we sweat heat
question: Why do we sweat when we are very hot?
answer: Sweat is liquid water from our skin. When sweat evaporates from our skin, it takes heat away from our body. This cools us down, which helps us stay at a healthy temperature on a hot day or after exercise.
keywords: sweat evaporates, takes heat from skin, cools body down

heading: Hot air balloon rises
question: Explain how a hot-air balloon rises into the sky.
answer: A burner heats the air inside the balloon. Hot air particles move faster and spread further apart, so the hot air becomes less dense than the cooler air outside. Less dense air rises, lifting the balloon upward. When the burner is turned off, the air cools, becomes denser, and the balloon sinks.
keywords: burner heats air, particles spread, hot air less dense, rises, denser air sinks

heading: Wind from sea breeze
question: On a sunny day at the beach, a cool breeze often blows from the sea to the land. Explain why.
answer: Land heats up faster than the sea in sunlight. The warm air over the land rises (it is less dense). To take its place, cooler air from over the sea moves in towards the land — this is the sea breeze. The movement of warm air up and cooler air in is a convection current.
keywords: land heats faster, warm air rises, cooler sea air moves in, sea breeze, convection

heading: Why dark cars hot
question: A black car left in the sun gets very hot inside. Explain.
answer: Black surfaces absorb most of the light and heat from the Sun. The metal body absorbs heat and conducts it to the inside. The trapped air heats up but cannot escape easily, so the inside of the car becomes very hot. A light-coloured car reflects more sunlight and stays cooler inside.
keywords: black absorbs most heat, metal conducts inside, trapped air heats up, very hot inside

heading: Drink cooler at home
question: When you take a cold drink out of the fridge and leave it on the table, the drink slowly becomes warmer. Why?
answer: Heat always flows from hotter to colder. The room air around the drink is warmer than the drink. So heat flows from the warmer air to the cooler drink. The drink gains heat and warms up, while the air around it loses a tiny bit of heat.
keywords: heat flows hot to cold, room warmer than drink, drink gains heat, warms up

heading: Convex lens — used in
question: Give two everyday uses of convex lenses.
answer: Magnifying glasses use a convex lens to make small things look bigger. Spectacles for long-sighted people use convex lenses to help them see nearby things clearly. Cameras and projectors use convex lenses to focus light to form a clear image. All these work because a convex lens bends light to converge.
keywords: magnifying glass, reading glasses, cameras, projectors, bends light

heading: Why mirror reverses
question: When you write a word on paper and hold it up to a mirror, the writing looks reversed. Why?
answer: Light from each point on the writing bounces straight off the mirror back to your eye. Points that are on your right appear to come from the right side of the mirror, so the image looks like a left-right reversed copy of the original. The mirror has not changed the writing — only the way the light reaches your eye.
keywords: light bounces straight back, left-right swapped, image reversed

heading: Why we see colour
question: A red apple looks red because it reflects only red light. What happens to the other colours from white light?
answer: White light is a mix of many colours. When white light hits the red apple, the apple absorbs all the other colours and reflects only the red. Our eyes see only the reflected red, so the apple looks red. A green leaf reflects only green; a black object absorbs all colours.
keywords: white light has many colours, object reflects its colour, absorbs the rest

heading: Why colourful soap bubble
question: Soap bubbles often look like they have rainbow colours. Briefly explain.
answer: A soap bubble has a very thin film of soapy water. When light hits the film, some bounces off the outer surface and some bounces off the inner surface. The two reflected lights combine and produce different colours depending on the thickness — that is why a bubble looks colourful and changes as the film moves.
keywords: thin film reflects light from outer and inner surface, combine to make colours

heading: Solid expansion
question: A metal lid is stuck on a glass jar. Pouring hot water on the lid helps loosen it. Explain.
answer: Hot water heats the metal lid. The metal expands a little when heated, becoming slightly wider. The glass jar heats up more slowly. So the lid is now a tiny bit bigger than before but the jar is the same size. The looser fit makes the lid easier to twist off.
keywords: metal expands when heated, jar slower, lid slightly wider, easier to twist

heading: Air takes space
question: How can you show that air takes up space? Describe a simple experiment.
answer: Push an empty plastic cup upside-down into a tank of water. The water does not fill the cup because air inside takes up the space. Tilt the cup slightly — bubbles of air escape and water then fills the cup. This shows air occupies space, even though it is invisible.
keywords: upside-down cup, water doesn't enter, air takes space, tilt to release bubbles

heading: Air has weight
question: How can you show that air has mass?
answer: Take two identical balloons. Weigh them in a balance with the air let out — they balance. Then blow up one balloon fully and place it back on the balance. The inflated balloon side goes down because the extra air inside has mass. So air does have mass.
keywords: two balloons, inflate one, heavier side, air has mass

heading: Sublimation example
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: Camphor and dry ice change directly from solid to gas, without first becoming liquid. What is this change called?
answer: This is called sublimation. The solid particles gain enough heat to escape directly into the air as a gas, skipping the liquid stage. Some students learn the term informally; the main point is the change of state is solid → gas directly.
keywords: sublimation, solid to gas directly, no liquid stage, camphor and dry ice

heading: Mirror condensation bathroom
topic: Water Cycle and Changes of State
question: Why does the bathroom mirror get foggy when you have a hot shower?
answer: Hot water in the shower produces a lot of water vapour. The vapour spreads through the bathroom. The mirror surface is cooler than the warm humid air. When the warm vapour touches the cooler mirror, it condenses into tiny water droplets, which together look like fog.
keywords: hot shower produces vapour, mirror cooler, vapour condenses to droplets, looks foggy

heading: Wedge changes direction
question: Why does dropping a heavy log onto a wedge split the log?
answer: When the log presses down on the wedge, the wedge changes the direction of the force. The downward force on the wedge becomes two sideways forces pushing apart at the angled sides of the wedge. These sideways forces push the wood apart and split the log.
keywords: wedge changes direction of force, downward force becomes sideways, splits wood

heading: Why heavier slower start
question: If you push a small empty box and a large heavy box with the same effort, the empty box moves faster. Why?
answer: Heavier objects have more mass. With the same pushing force, a heavier object accelerates less than a lighter one — it speeds up more slowly. With more mass to move, the same force has less effect, so the heavy box starts moving slower.
keywords: heavier has more mass, same force less acceleration, light box speeds up faster

heading: Brakes friction
question: How do bicycle brakes use friction to stop the bicycle?
answer: When you squeeze the brake, brake pads press against the rim of the spinning wheel. The friction between the pads and the rim acts opposite to the direction of motion of the rim. This frictional force slows the wheel down and stops the bicycle. Friction also turns the kinetic energy of the bike into heat in the pads and rim.
keywords: brake pads press wheel, friction opposes motion, slows wheel, kinetic to heat

heading: Series + closed circuit symbols
question: Draw or describe what a simple series circuit needs to light up two bulbs from one battery.
answer: You need: a battery, two bulbs, wires, and a switch. All four parts are connected in one single loop (a series circuit). When the switch is closed, current flows from the battery, through the first bulb, through the second bulb, back to the battery — and both bulbs light up.
keywords: battery, two bulbs, wires, switch, all in one loop, current through both

heading: Two bulbs series dimmer
question: When you add a second bulb in series, the first bulb becomes dimmer. Explain why.
answer: In series, both bulbs share the same battery energy. Each bulb gets less of the battery's voltage and current than if it were alone, so each one shines less brightly. The more bulbs you add in series, the dimmer each one becomes.
keywords: bulbs share voltage in series, each gets less, dimmer with more bulbs

heading: Identify magnetic material
question: How can you test if a material is magnetic, without using complicated equipment?
answer: Hold a magnet near the material. If the magnet attracts the material, then the material is magnetic. If there is no attraction, the material is non-magnetic. You can test small objects like paper clips, pins, coins, and pencils to find which are made of magnetic materials.
keywords: use a magnet, attracted means magnetic, not attracted means non-magnetic

heading: Why classify diagram
question: Why is it useful to use a classification key (a series of yes/no questions) to identify a living thing?
answer: A classification key narrows down what the living thing is by asking yes/no questions about its features one at a time. This makes identifying easier and quicker than trying to remember every animal or plant. The key also makes sure two people identifying the same living thing get the same answer, because they follow the same questions.
keywords: narrows down step by step, yes/no questions, quick to identify, same answer always

heading: Difference reptile amphibian
question: How can you tell a reptile from an amphibian?
answer: A reptile (like a lizard or snake) has dry, scaly skin and lays eggs on land. It breathes through lungs throughout its life. An amphibian (like a frog) has moist, smooth skin, lays eggs in water, and starts life breathing through gills before developing lungs as an adult.
keywords: reptile: dry scaly skin, eggs on land, lungs; amphibian: moist skin, eggs in water, gills then lungs

heading: Why bird not mammal
question: A bat flies like a bird, but it is grouped with mammals. Why?
answer: Mammals have fur or hair and feed their young with milk; the female gives birth to live young. A bat has fur, feeds its young with milk, and gives birth to live young — so it matches mammal features. A bird, by contrast, has feathers, lays eggs, and does not feed milk to its young. So bats are mammals even though they fly.
keywords: bat has fur and milk feeding, birds have feathers and eggs, bats fit mammals

heading: Why need pollination
question: Without pollination, a flowering plant cannot make seeds. Explain why.
answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another (or the same) flower. After pollination, the pollen grows down to the ovule and fertilises it — only then does the ovule develop into a seed. Without pollination, no fertilisation can happen, so no seeds are made and the plant cannot reproduce.
keywords: pollination transfers pollen, allows fertilisation, fertilised ovule becomes seed

heading: Animal pollination feature
question: Some flowers smell sweet and have nectar. Explain how these features help with pollination by insects.
answer: Sweet scents attract insects from far away. Nectar is a sugary liquid inside the flower that insects feed on. As the insect drinks the nectar, pollen sticks to its body. When it visits the next flower for more nectar, the pollen rubs off onto the stigma — pollination is done.
keywords: scent attracts insects, nectar is food, pollen sticks to insect, transferred next flower

heading: Pollen tube grows
question: Once pollen lands on the stigma, what must happen next for fertilisation?
answer: From the pollen grain, a pollen tube grows downward through the stigma and style into the ovary. Inside the tube travels a male cell. When it reaches the ovule, the male cell joins (fertilises) the egg cell inside the ovule. This is fertilisation, and the fertilised ovule then develops into a seed.
keywords: pollen tube grows down to ovary, male cell joins egg, fertilisation, seed forms

heading: Why animals reproduce sexually
question: Why is reproduction needed for a species to survive?
answer: Living things die — through age, accidents, predators or disease. If they did not produce new young, the species would die out. Reproduction makes new individuals so that the species continues from one generation to the next. Sexual reproduction also mixes features from two parents, creating variation that helps the species adapt.
keywords: individuals die, must produce new ones, species continues, variation from two parents

heading: Why we need energy
question: Why does the body need energy, even when you are sitting still?
answer: Even at rest, your body is doing many things: the heart beats, the lungs breathe, the brain thinks, food is being digested, cells are growing and repairing. All of these need energy from the food you eat. So you always use energy, just less than when you are moving.
keywords: even resting body uses energy, heart beats, lungs work, cells repair, from food

heading: Battery chemical
question: Why is a battery described as storing chemical energy?
answer: Inside a battery there are chemicals that, when connected in a circuit, react with each other. The reaction releases energy, which is converted into electrical energy that flows through the circuit. Because the energy is stored as a chemical reaction waiting to happen, we say the battery stores chemical energy.
keywords: chemicals react inside, releases energy, chemical to electrical, stored as chemicals

heading: Why energy from Sun
question: Almost all the energy on Earth comes from the Sun. Give two examples to support this.
answer: Plants use the Sun's light energy to make food (photosynthesis). Animals — including humans — get energy by eating plants or other animals that ate plants. Also, fossil fuels (oil, coal, gas) were once plants and animals that stored energy from the Sun long ago. Wind and rainfall — important for energy generation — also come from the Sun warming the Earth.
keywords: plants use sun for food, animals eat plants, fossil fuels were plants, wind and rain

heading: Heat from rubbing
question: Rubbing hands together makes them warm. Describe the energy conversion.
answer: Your muscles use chemical energy from food, converting it to kinetic energy as your hands move. The friction between your hands converts some of the kinetic energy into heat energy. So the chain is: chemical → kinetic → heat. Your hands feel warmer because of the heat produced.
keywords: chemical from food, kinetic rubbing, friction makes heat

heading: Population — what affects
question: Name two things that can cause the population of an animal to drop in its habitat.
answer: Loss of food (e.g. prey reduced), loss of habitat (e.g. forest cleared), too many predators, disease outbreak, pollution, and human hunting can all cause an animal's population to drop. keywords: less food, less habitat, more predators, disease, pollution, hunting

heading: Why food chain producer green
question: Why are green plants always the start of a food chain?
answer: Green plants are producers — only they can make their own food using sunlight (photosynthesis). They turn light energy from the Sun into chemical energy stored in food. Animals cannot do this. So all the energy in a food chain originally comes from green plants, which is why they sit at the start.
keywords: green plants make food from sunlight, only producers, energy starts here

heading: Why decomposers important
question: Fungi and bacteria are often called 'nature's recyclers'. Explain.
answer: When plants and animals die, fungi and bacteria break their bodies down. The minerals locked inside the dead matter are returned to the soil, where plants can take them up and grow. Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up, and plants would slowly starve of minerals. So decomposers recycle nutrients within the habitat.
keywords: break down dead matter, return minerals to soil, plants reuse, nutrient recycling

heading: Bird beak fits food
question: An eagle has a sharp hooked beak; a humming bird has a long thin beak; a duck has a wide flat beak. Explain how each beak suits the bird's food.
answer: Eagle: sharp hooked beak tears flesh — good for eating meat. Humming bird: long thin beak reaches deep into flowers for nectar. Duck: wide flat beak filters water and mud to catch small water plants and insects. Each beak is a structural adaptation that matches the food the bird eats.
keywords: eagle hooked: meat; humming long: nectar; duck flat: filter water; matches diet

heading: Behavioural — migration
question: Some birds fly to warmer countries every winter. What is this called and how does it help them?
answer: This behaviour is called migration. By moving to warmer places when their home is too cold, the birds avoid harsh winter conditions and find more food (which is hard to find in cold areas). They return to their home when the weather is warmer again. Migration helps the birds survive seasonal changes.
keywords: migration, avoid cold, find food in warmer places, return when warm

heading: Hibernation behaviour
question: Some animals, like the squirrel-like marmot, go into a deep sleep in winter. Why?
answer: In winter, the weather is very cold and food is hard to find. By going into a deep sleep (a form of hibernation), the animal's body activity slows down, so it uses very little energy. It lives off stored body fat until spring, when food returns. This helps it survive the harsh winter.

answer: Water is needed for many life processes: it dissolves substances so they can be transported around the body (e.g. blood is mostly water; sap is mostly water). Water helps reactions like digestion. Sweat (water) cools the body. Plants need water for photosynthesis. Without water, living things cannot survive long.
keywords: transports things in body, helps reactions, cools, plants need it for food, essential

heading: Why air needed for fire
question: A candle covered with a glass jar goes out after a short time. Explain.
answer: Burning needs oxygen from the air. Once the jar is placed over the candle, the small amount of air inside is gradually used up — the oxygen reacts with the wax to keep the flame going. When the oxygen runs out, the flame can no longer burn and goes out.
keywords: burning needs oxygen, sealed jar limited air, oxygen used up, flame goes out

heading: Why charcoal grills hot
question: Burning charcoal in a grill gets very hot. Where does the energy come from?
answer: Charcoal contains stored chemical energy (from when it was a tree that did photosynthesis long ago). When burned, the chemical energy is released as heat (and a little light). The heat warms the air and food above, cooking it. So the energy in a charcoal grill is sunlight, stored in the wood for a long time and now released.
keywords: charcoal has chemical energy (from sunlight long ago), burning releases heat, cooks food

heading: Why graph zero start
question: When drawing a graph, why should you usually start the axes at zero, not just at the first data value?
answer: Starting at zero gives a fair view of the data. If the axes start at a non-zero value, small changes can look much larger than they really are, which can mislead the reader. Starting at zero shows the true size of changes relative to the whole range.
keywords: axes start at zero for fair view, otherwise small changes look big, prevent misleading

heading: Why blind testing food
question: When testing if people prefer brand A or brand B chocolate, why might the tester hide the labels?
answer: Showing the labels could affect people's choices because some prefer one brand for non-taste reasons (price, advertising, familiarity). With labels hidden, people choose based only on taste. This makes the test fair — the result reflects taste preference, not brand preference.
keywords: labels can bias choice, hide for fair taste test, results show real preference

heading: Why nail pulls magnet
question: When an iron nail is brought close to a magnet, you can feel a pull even before they touch. What does this tell you about magnetic force?
answer: Magnetic force can act at a distance — through the air, without the magnet and nail touching. The nail is pulled toward the magnet by the magnetic force long before contact. This is different from a push or pull that you make with your hand, which needs touching.
keywords: magnetic force acts at distance, no touching needed, attracts iron through air

heading: Friction wood floor walking
question: Walking on a wood floor feels safe, but walking on the same floor after polishing feels slippery. Why?
answer: An unpolished floor has small rough patches that grip the soles of shoes — friction is high, so you don't slip. Polishing smooths the floor, reducing friction. With less friction, your shoes can slide more easily — you may slip. That's why polished floors are sometimes marked 'caution'.
keywords: rough floor more friction, polished smooth, less friction, slippery

heading: Why see through window
question: Why can you see through a window pane but not through a wall, even though both stop wind?
answer: Glass in a window is transparent — light passes through it almost completely, so you see what's on the other side. A wall is opaque — light cannot pass through, so you cannot see anything beyond it. Both block wind, but only transparent materials let light through.
keywords: glass transparent lets light through, wall opaque blocks light, both block air

heading: Why eyes need light
question: Why do we need a light on at night to read a book?
answer: We see by light reflected off objects into our eyes. In the dark, no light reaches the book and so no light reflects off the words into our eyes — we cannot see. Turning on a light gives the book something to reflect; light from the page then enters our eyes and we can read.
keywords: see by reflected light, dark = no light, light reflects off page, eyes see

heading: Why blowing on food
question: Why does blowing on hot soup help cool it down?
answer: Blowing moves the warm air just above the soup away, replacing it with cooler air. Heat from the soup can pass into the new cooler air faster, so the soup loses heat more quickly and cools down. Blowing also helps water vapour evaporate from the surface, which also takes heat away.
keywords: moves warm air away, fresh cool air, faster heat loss, evaporation takes heat

heading: Why metal handle covered
question: Some metal kettles have a plastic-covered handle. Why?

keywords: plastic poor conductor, stops heat passing to hand, safe to hold metal kettle

heading: Energy in solar oven

heading: Walking energy

heading: Why straws drink

heading: Why ice cubes float
question: Ice cubes float on water. What does this tell us?

heading: Why menstrual lining shed

heading: Why same observer

heading: Why thermometer at eye level
